raw_response:
It's early October and I need to get my winter crops in the ground before the soil gets too cold. I've been farming these 50 mu for 15 years now — started when I was 21 right after finishing middle school. With 7 people in the house, including my parents who can still help out and my two kids who are in school, I need steady income but I also can't afford to gamble everything on one crop. That's why my backbone is the wheat-maize double crop on 30 mu. It's not the highest profit, but it's reliable.

I'm planting Jinmai 22, an improved wheat variety that's done well here the last few years. For fertilizer, I'm putting down about 20 kg of N per mu total — the extension station guy keeps saying I could push to 22 or 25, but I learned my lesson two years ago when I went heavy and then a windy spring came and the wheat lodged bad. I'll split it: compound fertilizer as base at planting, then topdress urea at jointing in late March if the wheat looks green enough. Four irrigations from my well — overwinter water, jointing, heading, and filling. The pump electricity isn't cheap, but dry wheat is dead wheat, so I don't skip it.

The maize goes on that same 30 mu right after wheat harvest in early June. That week is always chaos — the window between wheat coming off and maize needing to be in is usually less than seven days. I hire a combine and a corn planter because doing it by hand would mean planting too late. Hybrid seed, about 18 kg N per mu, and I'll side-dress urea when the maize is knee-high in July. Two irrigations should be enough if the summer rains are normal, but I'll watch the sky — the flowering stage in July is when you can't let it go dry.

My garlic is on 5 mu in the south plot where the soil is looser and drains better. I'm using my own saved cloves from last year's best bulbs — saves me seed money and I know they don't have disease. Garlic is a fertilizer hog, especially potassium, so I push more K there than anywhere else. Five irrigations, easy. Onions are 4 mu, transplanted in March; cabbage is 4 mu of an early variety so I can hit the market before the June glut; chili is 4 mu, which is labor hell with all the picking, but my wife and my mother handle most of that, and I hire a few local women during peak harvest when the price is good. Stevia I've got 3 mu — a buyer from Shandong comes every year, so it's boring but reliable. Low fertilizer, just keep it irrigated and cut it three times.

Total cash I'm putting into inputs this year is about 38,500 yuan. That's a lot, but with 50 mu I can spread the risk. Still, I'm keeping a few thousand yuan back in my pocket — never put every yuan in the ground. If the pump breaks or someone gets sick, I need cash in hand. The vegetables can pay better than grain, but one bad market price and you're stuck. So I balance: grain for stability, vegetables for profit.
